what: Offline reviewer catch-rate replay (2026-10-15): every replayable review round of 7 harvested runs, its reviewed patch state graded against the hidden tests (VM Docker grader, wf-grader:1), then only the reviewer re-run with the Phase 3 CPU pool config. Catch = REVISE on a hidden-test-failing state; false alarm = REVISE on a passing state.
replayed_reviewer: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on CPU worker llmbench01 (C2T10), --read-first --defects-only, default step cap (20) -- the p3-gp-1 pool reviewer
original_reviewers: per source run: qwen3.8 (router) for w3-2-t, p3-gp-1 pool = same CPU reviewer, the rest GPU lead Qwen3.6/qwen3.8 variants (see catch-rate inventory)
findings: The CPU reviewer catches 12 of 35 failing states (34%) and raises 25 false alarms on 123 passing states (20%): a REVISE from it is right about 1 time in 3.
The original reviewers (mostly GPU) catch 19 of 35 (54%) with 34 of 123 false alarms (28%) on the same states -- better at catching, still wrong on about 2 of 3 REVISEs.

Failing states cluster in 6 tasks; 26 of 35 fail exactly one hidden test (an edge case the reviewer cannot see). The CPU reviewer misses w2-05 almost always (1 of 11) where the GPU reviewers catch it (8 of 11), and never catches w2-16.
States are not independent (the same task's bug recurs across runs), so the effective sample is about 6 distinct bugs; the direction is clear, the exact rates are not.
verdict: CPU review as configured does not earn its place for quality: it catches a third of the bad patches and its REVISEs are mostly wrong. Keep S (GPU alone) as the default; keep --review-pool available but off. The GPU reviewer is better but still low-precision; the misses are single hidden edge cases, so the next lever is not more review of the diff but a reviewer that exercises the code (writes and runs targeted edge-case tests), measured offline on these same 158 labelled states.
